newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Plebiscite urged to end Brazil re-election saga.
newsitem.headline: Plebiscite urged to end Brazil re-election saga.

text.p: While politicians battle over whether President Fernando Henrique Cardoso should be allowed to run for re-election, some prominent figures believe the issue should be handed over to the Brazilian voters.

Journalists, businessmen and even a Supreme Court justice argue a national plebiscite would be the most transparent and democratic way to decide if the constitution should be altered to allow elected officials to run for a second term in office.

"As a citizen I believe a politician who has proven to be a competent administrator ought to be given an opportunity to seek a second term," said Marco Aurelio de Mello, a Supreme Court Justice who has raised eyebrows because of his outspoken views over the re-election question.
"However, if we are willing to consider such an important change in our constitution, wouldn't it be appropiate to consult the people?" he said.
This week President Cardoso saw his re-election bid stalled in Congress by opponents who claim the government is scheming to perpetuate itself in office.
The government says its political rivals are not opposed to re-election in principle but are obstructing the amendment in the hope of obtaining some political advantage.
Many commentators, including Mello, believe the re-election debate has been debased and complain the amendment has been reduced to political bargaining chip.
They argue a national plebiscite would raise the level of the debate, isolating it from the short term objectives of party politics.
Electoral court officials say a plebiscite could be quickly organized and held by late April if a law authorizing the vote were approved by Congress by mid-February.
Recent opinion polls show 65 percent of the population approve a re-election amendment while 35 percent oppose it, a sign Cardoso has strong public support on the issue.

"Prudence and political stability would advise the president to abandon the battle in Congress, and tie his future to a plebiscite," Folha de Sao Paulo journalist Elio Gaspari wrote in his column this week.

However some well-known experienced political analysts think this view is naive. They say that while at present it appears certain that Cardoso would win a re-election plebiscite, in the run-up period before the vote the president would remain dangerously exposed to attacks from his political rivals.

"A national plebiscite is a two-edged sword. It would probably not take place before the middle of the year and could develop into a full-fledged electoral campaign," said political analyst Bolivar Lamounier.

While Cardoso has repeatedly stated he would prefer to obtain the re-election amendment with congressional approval, he has hinted at the possibility of calling a plebiscite as a way of softening his opposition in Congress.

Analysts say a plebiscite in which Cardoso were victorious would be a disaster for the opposition because not only would they lose all their bargaining power, it would also cast them into the political wilderness until Cardoso left office.

"The government would only call a plebiscite as a matter last resort," said political analyst Ricardo Pedreira. "It would rather win the re-election amendment by having it voted in Congress. But if that doesn't happen a plebiscite may be the only alternative."
